Until this game is much improved, I can't really recommend it because of two glaring issues: -Reading reviews, I realized only the French dictionary had received much love, but even that one, which should be the most developped, is very lacking, which leads to very frustrating situations when even relatively common words aren't allowed. -The roguelike part is utterly embryonic and ludicrously unbalanced: you only get one modifier picked from a random panel of three every round. Problem is, some modifiers are extremely powerful and pretty much guarantee a smooth run without any combos if you draw them in the first rounds; most others are insignificant, extremely situational or even slightly detrimental, without any build potential in most cases; very few of those modifiers gel together to be conducive to satisfying combos. So basically, with only three picks per round and no other mechanics, it's just a basic lottery at this point, there's usually no way to compensate for poor draws with a good choice of words or strategic planning. Scrabble has more depth. There's potential, but there's a long road ahead for this to become a good game.

Wordatro is one of those games that you see someone else play and are like "huh, this looks interesting. Let me give it a try." You buy it, you install it, and then you realise that hours of your day has gone by as you try to not only remember words in the English language (or whatever language you speak), while also trying to think about your strategy and letter placement. The game's a lot more complicated than it lets on. There is a ridiculous amount of strategy required to get good at this game that will likely take hundreds, if not thousands, of hours to perfect. If you like your Scrabble / Words With Friends / Other word games not listed above, play this. Because who needs friends when you have the comforting sound of the numbers going up in your videogame?

Wordatro is a very fun word game with a rougelike premise. The game is pretty well made, with crisp design and gameplay. Difficulties also vary depending on which mode you play, from a super easy mode to pro mode (which is really hard). There is also a daily challenge that is the same for everyone. The only downside to Wordatro is that there isn't enough unique things or challenges to work towards after you already go through the difficulties. In other words, the game starts to get a bit too repetitive. Overall, worth giving this a shot. I enjoyed it while I was playing it.

I'm glad this game was in a charity bundle because I don't think it's worth buying on its own. It feels rather unfinished and it's disappointing to see that since it was released in June 2025, it's only gotten one bug fix update and no other changes besides the removal of a game mode. Surely a game called Wordatro wasn't only made to quickly cash in on the popularity of a certain similar-sounding game? (spoiler: it was) The crux of the issue--which is also the main point of most of the negative reviews I read--is how easy it is to get stuck with a hand full of vowels worth basically no points even if you do find a way to string them into a word, and the bonuses are way too small or situational to make up for it as the score required keeps growing exponentially. The game gives you two rerolls that each allow you to exchange three letters, but there is nothing stopping you from getting those same letters back (or at least, different vowels--I could be wrong about getting the same letters back). Another issue is that the dictionary feels kind of arbitrary, disallowing words like "LAGGY" for not being real dictionary words yet allowing many proper nouns or names. For example, during the very first round of the tutorial, I was given the letters [b]A A A A P P R S U X[/b] (in my experience, this is what the average hand looks like in terms of vowel count). Despite "AURAS" being the best possible word I could think of, the game suggested I make the word "AARU". Do you know what this word means? Because I sure don't. It turns out it's the ancient Egyptian name for the Field of Reeds. Allowing these kinds of "words" is harmful because assuming there's some sort of algorithm that ensures you can always make [i]some[/i] word with the new letters you get (I'm not actually sure if there is), the game must implicitly assume you will know these terms. Some of the QoL I'd expect also isn't really there. It would be great if the game would show you the definitions of the words you submit since you're going to be guessing sometimes, but it doesn't. When you Shift + type to send letters to the reroll area, it sends your special tiles instead of your normal ones. The ability to see how many points you would earn for the word you're about to submit would be quite nice, but is missing--though the information is hardly a secret since you can always painstakingly add up the points, check your bonuses, and factor in the multipliers if you really want to (probably missing a bonus somewhere along the way, resulting in catastrophe). All in all, this game fell flat for me since even if you have a great vocabulary, you're too often at the mercy of your letter draws with little recourse if things don't go your way.

After playing this game for a few hours, it's kind of fun a fun twist on Scrabble and Balatro, but ultimately fails at being a decent Balatro-like, like the game's title suggests. There doesn't feel like there's a lot of room for replayability or progression beyond beating a run. You can change the difficulty level, but I never really felt rewarded in beating a run, because you don't really seem to unlock anything to make future runs easier or add more challenge or strategy. I also think being able to choose the difficulty and do an easy run lessens the challenge of it being a roguelike. Is it really a roguelike if I can beat an easy run first-try? I'm only 3 hours into this game (at the time of writing this) and have already beat several runs on several difficulties. It's not really the kind of experience I expect from a game labelled as a roguelike. Beyond choosing the difficulty for the run, there's also a daily challenge run and scoreboard which is kind of fun, and I would like to see more variation in gameplay like that. There also doesn't seem to be a lot of variety in upgrades, and many of the instructions on what each of these upgrades do can be very confusing in how they are worded. Oftentimes I chose an upgrade or used a special letter without truly understanding what it does until several runs in. You also draw WAY too many vowels compared to consonants. So much so that there's been too many times that it would be pretty impossible to even try making a word because I've got a hand with something like 3 A's and 3 I's and 2 U's and maybe a J and a G...it just feels super unbalanced. I think it's a decent game to open up and play once in a while for 30 minutes if you've got nothing else to play and also enjoy games like Scrabble, but if I'm being honest, I'd say just go play Balatro instead.

Wordatro! is a basic letter arranging word game that looks and feels like a mobile app despite being on Steam. Wow, the earnings meeting is going to be hilarious when the managers ask what revenue came in from the app stores. This is basically the weakest ripoff of Scrabble I've ever seen. The developer ripped off the branding and trademarked name of the popular poker game, Balatro, blatantly stealing someone else's concept there, and slapped it on Scrabble but with multiplayer and most of the other game elements removed. So instead of the Scrabble grid you just have a line, and you make words without the fuss of needing them to connect to other words... told you it was dumbed down. So yeah, not much of a game here. Incredibly shallow stuff. From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard. There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks. There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display. There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision. The game interface is mostly just text boxes/dialogs and features mostly static, barely animated 2D images, the kind of thing you expect to see in browser/HTML games from the 1990s. While that might be fine for the 1990s, gaming has evolved a lot since then, the ATI Rage became mainstream in 1996... it's 2026, and that kind of thing just won't fly anymore, it's just not visually up to scratch. The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just iPhone screen tapping stuff. The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction. You'll get none of that here. This is indistinguishable from a mobile app, but they put this on Steam instead of the app stores by mistake. Was it rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all)?. Regardless, for all intents and purposes Wordatro! might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities. It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers. We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones. Those technical issues put this game beneath what is expected from a contemporary, professionally developed PC game. So, should you buy this game? Is this one of the best of the 140,000+ games on Steam? Wordatro! has the preposterous price of around $10 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam. Ten bucks for a mobile app in exile that's just a dumbed down single player version of Scrabble. $10 for something slightly worse than the kinds of games you can play for free on mobile. Jesus wept... that's a cash grab. For comparison, the $10 asking price for this game could get you games like "Deep Rock Galactic", "Far Cry 5" or "Mirror's Edge". Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.

Wish I could give an 'eh' recommendation. It's a solid enough game, but there's very little replay value, relies way too much on RNG (as others have said, you very often pull entire hands of vowels) with very little ability to express skill. The bonuses simply *feel* weak, no matter how strong they might be, and the low amount of rerolls and tries ('energy') per round basically mean you have to play perfectly to manage anything, especially on the higher difficulties (which only really reduce how many rerolls and energy you get for winning a hand...and since both of those carry over hand to hand, it's very easy to get into a fast death spiral after one bad play). I haven't played Balatro so I can't compare it to that.

This game's alright enough, I had a moderate amount of fun beating each difficulty level and doing some extra challenge achievements. I think its biggest problem is its own limited scope - when you only have to beat (at most) 10 rounds, only have (at first) 10 letters to work with, and only get (at first) 9 tiles to build a word with, it just doesn't feel like you get a whole lot of creativity to work with. The tight challenge in the harder difficulties (e.g. starting out with only 2 energy and 1 refresh in the hardest) is honestly fairly cool, but it also sticks you in a loop of immediately resetting until you get good enough RNG. When the RNG does hit, it can feel really good; you just have to grind for it a bit. There's also just some basic technical issues - typos in achievements, lack of any sort of indication in the UI that you've completed a game mode before, and the fact that when I first booted it on PC (after playing on steam deck for a while last year), the language and dictionary selection both said something in French that I think meant "Sample Text", Overall, it is fun enough, and the devs clearly put in the effort to come up with some really good ideas, but it still lacks in quite a few areas imo.
